parts.problem_md:
**Depth study B: Germany, 1918–45**

Discuss the extent to which life improved for the German people in the 1920s.
parts.solution_md:
Between 1924 and 1929 the Weimar Republic gave many Germans a standard of living and a personal freedom they had never had under the Kaiser. Whether life improved depends heavily on which Germans are being discussed [R].

The clearest improvement was in living standards for workers in towns and cities. Workers' real wages rose 25% between 1925 and 1928, and the working week fell from 50 hours in 1925 to 46 in 1927 [R]. The Unemployment Insurance Act of 1927 took 3% of the wages of 16.4 million workers and paid 60 Reichsmarks a week to anyone out of work or too ill to work [R]. Housing improved, with private companies building 37,000 homes between 1925 and 1929 and building associations a further 64,000, while over 1.3 million widows and ex-soldiers received a pension under the Reich Pension Law [R]. This was the beginning of a German welfare state, and it meant that for the first time illness or unemployment did not automatically mean destitution [E].

A second facet is the position of women, where the legal gains were genuine. The Weimar Constitution gave every woman over 21 the vote on the same terms as men, which was rare in Europe, and Article 119 declared marriage an equal legal partnership [R]. Women voted in large numbers, with turnout around 90%, and 111 women were elected to the Reichstag in 1920 [R]. More women worked as teachers and doctors, and the 'New Woman' of the 1920s could work, dress and behave with a freedom previous generations had never known [E].

A third facet is culture, which flourished as never before. The government gave grants to artists and to organisations such as theatres and libraries, and supported rather than censored new work [R]. The Bauhaus movement was founded by Walter Gropius in 1919 and taught by figures such as Paul Klee, artists including Otto Dix and George Grosz produced work that questioned German society, and by 1929 there were roughly 500 cinemas in Germany [R]. The government funded Fritz Lang's Metropolis in 1926 through UFA at a cost of 5 million Reichsmarks, and Berlin's cabarets and nightclubs made the city famous [R]. Ordinary Germans had access to art, film and nightlife that had simply not existed a decade earlier [E].

However, the countryside was left behind. There was a clear divide between the industrial and agricultural working classes, and it was town and city workers who benefited from the reforms [R]. High debt, low prices and rising taxes damaged living standards in farming communities, so that by 1929 the income of agricultural workers was 44% below the national average [R]. Unemployment also remained at one million throughout the so-called Golden Age [R]. For a substantial part of the population the 1920s were not a recovery at all [A].

Women's gains were also narrower than they appeared. The proportion of women in employment fell from 75% in 1918 to 36% by 1925, roughly the pre-war level; employers ignored Article 119 and chose men; and women in work were paid 33% less than men doing the same job [R]. Society still expected a woman to leave her job on marriage, and Germany had only 36 female judges by 1933 [R]. The right to vote had been won, but the right to a career largely had not [A].

The cultural changes also made enemies, which mattered politically. The right-wing vilified the 'New Woman' for destroying the traditional family, Hitler blamed her for working-class unemployment, and male-dominated trade unions resented 'double earners' [R]. The KPD saw funding for the arts as money taken from workers who needed it, while the NSDAP argued that Weimar culture was destroying German traditions and causing moral decline [R]. Improvements that a large minority actively resented were storing up trouble rather than building loyalty [A].

Life improved substantially, but for a narrower group than the phrase 'Golden Age' suggests. For an urban worker, and especially for a young unmarried woman in a city, the years 1924 to 1929 brought real gains in wages, security, rights and culture [A]. For a farmer, for the million who remained unemployed, and for most married women hoping to keep a job, very little changed. The improvements were also concentrated where they created most resentment, so the Republic's greatest social achievements handed its enemies their most effective arguments. Life improved to a large extent for some Germans and hardly at all for others, and that division is the most important thing about the decade [A].

parts.problem_md:
**Depth study B: Germany, 1918–45**

Discuss the importance of Gustav Stresemann to the recovery of the Weimar Republic.
parts.solution_md:
Gustav Stresemann was chancellor for only three months, from August to November 1923, and foreign minister until his death on 3 October 1929. In that time Germany went from a worthless currency and a foreign army on its soil to membership of the League of Nations. The question is how much of that recovery belonged to him [R].

The first facet is the currency, and here his importance is hard to dispute. When he took office the mark had collapsed: the largest note was for 100 trillion marks and the government believed 400.3 billion trillion marks were in circulation [R]. In November 1923 Stresemann introduced the Rentenmark, worth a trillion old marks, backed it with a new state-owned Rentenbank and tied it to the gold standard so that European countries would trust it [R]. This was decisive because a currency nobody accepts makes trade impossible; restoring one that foreign markets respected allowed German businesses to buy and sell abroad again, which is the precondition for every other recovery that followed [E]. He also ended the passive resistance in the Ruhr, restoring German production, and French and Belgian troops left the region in 1925 [R]. Stresemann had set himself three aims on taking office: to control inflation, to regain Europe's respect and to reduce support for extremist parties, and the currency reform served all three [R].

The second facet is reparations, where his importance is more qualified. Stresemann negotiated the Dawes Plan of 1924, which set payments at 50 million pounds a year and brought American investment into German industry, and the Young Plan of 1929, which cut total reparations to 2 billion pounds and extended repayment over 59 years [R]. These plans genuinely eased the burden and improved relations with France [E]. But the money was American, not German, and the arrangement left Germany dependent on the United States [A]. Stresemann understood this himself, warning in 1929 that Germany was 'dancing on a volcano' [R]. His achievement here was to buy time rather than to solve the problem, and when the Wall Street Crash came the borrowed prosperity vanished [A].

The third facet is Germany's international position, and this was arguably his greatest success. The Treaty of Versailles had banned Germany from the League of Nations and excluded it from world politics [R]. Stresemann negotiated the Locarno Treaties in December 1925, obtained German membership of the League in September 1926 with a seat on its Council, and signed the Kellogg-Briand Pact in August 1928 alongside 61 other countries, winning the Nobel Peace Prize in 1926 [R]. This mattered because it reversed the most humiliating element of the settlement without firing a shot, and it made Germany a respectable state able to enter treaties as an equal [E].

The fourth facet is domestic politics, where the effects were real but not his alone. Support for extremist parties fell: the Nazi vote declined at every election between 1924 and 1928 while the SPD gained steadily, there were no political assassinations between 1924 and 1929, and only six coalition governments formed in those five years, far fewer than before [R]. Success abroad gave Germans a reason to believe the Republic could deliver [E]. Yet Hindenburg's election as president in 1925 also increased right-wing middle-class support for the Republic, and that owed nothing to Stresemann [A]. Extremist parties still held 13% of the vote, and nationalists remained angry that the government kept following the Treaty of Versailles [R].

Stresemann was the most important single figure in the Republic's recovery, but his importance lies in stabilisation rather than in cure. The Rentenmark was his, the treaties were his, and the political calm of 1924 to 1929 followed from both; no other individual contributed anything comparable [A]. A stronger reading is that a Republic kept going by foreign success needed ever more of it. That judgement is too harsh, since Germany in 1923 needed rescuing before it could be reformed. The fairest conclusion is that Stresemann was indispensable to the recovery and insufficient for its survival: he made the Republic work, but he could not make it independent of American money, and it was that dependence, not his policies, which killed it [A].

parts.problem_md:
**Depth study B: Germany, 1918–45**

Write an account of Germany's economic recovery between 1923 and 1929.
parts.solution_md:
When Gustav Stresemann became chancellor in August 1923 the German economy had crashed. The French invasion of the Ruhr had caused hyperinflation and the mark was worthless: the largest note was for 100 trillion marks, and the government believed there were 400.3 billion trillion marks in circulation [R]. Stresemann had three aims: to bring inflation under control, to regain Europe's respect, and to minimise support for extremist parties [D].

His first step was a new currency. In November 1923 he created the Rentenmark, where one Rentenmark was the equivalent of a trillion old marks, and established a new state-owned bank, the Rentenbank, at which the public exchanged their old notes [R]. The Rentenmark was a gold standard currency, meaning its value matched the price of gold, which European countries trusted [D]. In August 1924 the government created the Reichsbank to control the currency and renamed it the Reichsmark [R]. Stresemann also ended the passive resistance in the Ruhr, which increased Germany's production capability, and French and Belgian soldiers left the Ruhr in 1925 [R].

Reparations were then restructured twice. The Dawes Plan of April 1924 set reparations at 50 million pounds a year and brought American money into German industry, with US banks lending directly to German businesses [R]. It improved relations with France and improved trade and employment, but it also left Germany in debt to the USA [D]. The Young Plan of August 1929 went further, reducing total reparations to 2 billion pounds and extending the repayment period to 59 years, which allowed the government to lower taxes on its citizens [R]. Both plans angered extremist parties, who argued that Germany should not be repaying reparations produced by a corrupt treaty at all [D].

The effects were visible in ordinary life. Workers' real wages rose 25% between 1925 and 1928, and the working week fell from 50 hours in 1925 to 46 hours in 1927 [R]. The Unemployment Insurance Act of 1927 diverted 3% of the wages of 16.4 million workers into a fund which paid 60 Reichsmarks a week to anyone unemployed or unable to work through ill health [R]. Housing improved as the Lander used foreign loans and a 15% rent tax to fund building, so that private companies built 37,000 new homes between 1925 and 1929 while building associations constructed 64,000 [R]. Over 1.3 million widows and ex-soldiers received a war pension under the Reich Pension Law [R].

The recovery was uneven. Unemployment remained at one million throughout the period, and the divide between rich and poor persisted [R]. Farmers struggled particularly badly with low prices, and by 1929 the income of agricultural workers was 44% below the national average [R]. Germany's new prosperity also rested on American loans, which is why Stresemann said in 1929 that Germany was 'dancing on a volcano' [D].

parts.problem_md:
**Depth study B: Germany, 1918–45**

Write an account of the German Revolution of 1918.
parts.solution_md:
By the autumn of 1918 Germany could not continue the war. Between 1914 and 1918 two million German soldiers had died and four million more had been wounded, among them Adolf Hitler, temporarily blinded by mustard gas in October 1918 [R]. Germany's debt had trebled from 50 billion marks in 1914 to 150 billion marks in 1918 [R]. The British Navy had blockaded German ports so that no food from overseas could enter the country, and the German people were near starvation [D].

Unrest then spread from the ports across the country. In October 1918 the German navy mutinied at Kiel and Hamburg [R]. On 7 November the workers of Munich, the capital of Bavaria, held a general strike and announced that they were a separate communist state [R]. In Hanover soldiers joined workers and rioted in the streets, and in Berlin there were mass protests [R]. Many towns set up councils of workers and soldiers to replace the Kaiser's official local authorities, so the old system of government was being dismantled from below [D]. Once the capital was lost, the Kaiser had lost control of the whole country [D].

The Kaiser's position collapsed within days. On 9 November 1918 his military advisers told him he must abdicate in order to stop the civil unrest [R]. Max von Baden, whom the Kaiser had appointed as Chancellor on 3 October, announced the abdication without the Kaiser's consent or knowledge [R]. The following day the Kaiser escaped from Germany by train and arrived in the Netherlands [R].

A new government was assembled immediately. Max von Baden resigned and offered the chancellorship to Friedrich Ebert, the leader of the Social Democratic Party, who accepted [R]. On 10 November Ebert worked with General Groener and the army to suppress the communist rioters, dismissed the old Reichstag, and created a Council of People's Representatives, six politicians who would govern Germany until elections could be held [R]. The Republic's first act was to sign the armistice on 11 November, ending the First World War [R]. To hold the new state together Ebert promised the trade unions an eight-hour working day, promised big business that their property would not be nationalised, and promised General Groener that the army would not be reformed [D]. The civil servants who had served the Kaiser continued their work alongside the new workers' councils [D]. Elections for a National Assembly were held on 19 January 1919, with a turnout of 82%; the SPD won 40% of the vote and the Centre Party 20%, both moderate parties [R]. In February 1919 Ebert was elected as Germany's first president, and the Assembly met at Weimar, away from the unrest in Berlin, to write a new constitution [R].

parts.problem_md:
**The Weimar Republic lasted from 1919 until 1933.**

'The Weimar Republic was doomed from the start.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
parts.solution_md:
The Republic's founding problems were real, but it survived them and recovered. What destroyed it came later, and from outside Germany [R].

It was born owning a defeat it had not caused. The Weimar government's first act was to sign the armistice, and its politicians were branded 'November Criminals' who had committed a 'dolchstoss', because the Allies had never defeated the German Army in battle [R]. It then had to sign the Treaty of Versailles, accepting blame under Article 231 and reparations of 132 billion gold marks [R]. No new government could easily survive being permanently identified with national humiliation [E].

Its constitution also built in weakness. Proportional representation meant no party ever won a majority, producing nine coalition governments between 1919 and 1923, while Article 48 let the chancellor bypass the Reichstag entirely, and Ebert used it 63 times in 1923-24 [R]. Extremists attacked from both sides, and the government relied on force to hold power [E].

However, the Republic recovered strongly after 1923. Stresemann replaced the worthless mark with the Rentenmark in November 1923, negotiated the Dawes and Young Plans, brought Germany into the League of Nations in 1926 and signed the Kellogg-Briand Pact in 1928 [R]. Real wages rose 25% between 1925 and 1928 and the working week fell from 50 hours to 46 [R]. A doomed state does not stabilise its currency and rejoin the international community within three years [A].

Politics stabilised too. There were no political assassinations between 1924 and 1929, only six coalition governments formed in that period, and support for the Nazis fell at every election between 1924 and 1928 [R]. Voters were turning towards moderate parties, not away from them [A].

The statement is therefore true only to a limited extent. The flaws were genuine and they explain how quickly the Republic fell once it was tested again [A]. But it was not doomed: it was fragile, and it depended on prosperity. Stresemann said in 1929 that Germany was 'dancing on a volcano' because recovery rested on American loans. It was the Wall Street Crash, not 1919, that made the collapse certain [A].

parts.problem_md:
**The Weimar Republic was attacked from both the left and the right.**

Which was the greater threat to the Weimar Republic: the Spartacist Uprising or the Kapp Putsch? Explain your answer.
parts.solution_md:
The Spartacists wanted a different Germany; the Freikorps wanted a different government. That distinction decides which was the greater danger [R].

The Spartacist Uprising threatened the Republic's survival at its weakest moment. Beginning on 4 January 1919, before the Republic had even been elected, it put over 100,000 workers on the streets of Berlin and seized the government's newspaper and telegraph offices [R]. To defeat the rising Ebert had to use the Freikorps, armed right-wing ex-soldiers who hated communists, and the killing of Luxemburg and Liebknecht on 16 January made the left permanent enemies of the SPD [R]. The Republic therefore began by arming the very people who would attack it next, and by dividing the left against itself [A].

The Kapp Putsch, however, came from inside the state's own forces. In March 1920 Ebert planned to disband the Freikorps units in Berlin, so 5,000 of them under Wolfgang Kapp attempted to overthrow the government and invited the Kaiser to return [R]. The army would not fire on them, so the elected government had to flee its own capital [E].

Yet Kapp collapsed quickly. The lower classes would not support the Kaiser's return, having gained rights since his abdication, so the workers called a general strike which cut Berlin's gas, electricity, water and public transport, and after four days Kapp left the city [R]. Right-wing violence continued, with 376 political assassinations in the Republic's first three years [R].

The Kapp Putsch was the greater threat. The Spartacists were more visible and came first, but they were defeated by force in nine days and never had mass support beyond Berlin [A]. Kapp exposed something worse: the Republic could not rely on its own army, and was saved not by the state but by workers choosing to strike. A government whose survival depends on its opponents' unpopularity rather than on its own strength has a permanent weakness, and the right kept its weapons afterwards [A].

parts.problem_md:
**The National Assembly completed the Weimar Constitution in 1919.**

How successful was the Weimar Constitution? Explain your answer.
parts.solution_md:
The Weimar Constitution gave Germany the most democratic system in Europe. Whether it worked depends on whether a democracy that cannot govern is a success [R].

Its protections were genuine. Written at Weimar in February 1919 and passed by 262 votes to 75, it gave every man and woman over 21 the vote, elected the Reichstag every four years and the president every seven, and used proportional representation so that one seat was awarded for every 60,000 votes [R]. Smaller parties were therefore represented rather than excluded, and no single group could seize the state, since the president chose the chancellor but the public chose the president [E].

It also spread power deliberately. The Reichstag and the Reichsrat worked together, the Lander kept control of schools and the police, and the Reichsrat could challenge laws unless two-thirds of the Reichstag overruled it [R]. For a country that had never had a written constitution under the Kaiser, who made and changed laws as he pleased, this was a transformation [E].

However, proportional representation made government almost impossible. No single party ever won a majority in the Reichstag, and there were nine coalition governments between 1919 and 1923 alone [R]. Policies lacked vision and took far longer to pass, so the system that fairly represented every opinion could rarely act on any of them [A].

Article 48 then supplied the escape route. It allowed the chancellor to ask the president to pass emergency laws without the Reichstag, and Ebert used it 63 times between 1923 and 1924 [R]. A clause meant for genuine emergencies became the ordinary way of governing, and its abuse continued into the 1930s [A].

The constitution was therefore successful only to a limited extent. As a statement of rights it was admirable, and the freedoms it created were real [A]. But a constitution is judged by whether it lets a country be governed, and this one produced deadlock so reliably that its own presidents had to bypass it. It handed later politicians a legal method of ruling without parliament, which is the opposite of what its authors intended [A].

parts.problem_md:
**Stresemann became Germany's foreign minister in November 1923.**

One reason was that his treaties ended Germany's isolation. As foreign minister from November 1923 Stresemann negotiated the Locarno Treaties in December 1925, obtained German membership of the League of Nations in September 1926 with a seat on its Council, and signed the Kellogg-Briand Pact in August 1928 alongside 61 other countries [R]. **The new German government signed the armistice in November 1918.**

parts.solution_md:
One reason was that most Germans did not believe they had lost the war. The Allies had not defeated the German Army in battle, and the army had retreated in November 1918 rather than being destroyed [R]. parts.problem_md: Discuss the impact of the Weimar Constitution on the stability of the Republic.
parts.solution_md:
**The first facet is the democratic legitimacy the constitution created.** The National Assembly met at Weimar in February 1919 and took six months to write the constitution, which passed by 262 votes to 75. It gave the vote to all men and women aged 21 and over, an elected Reichstag every four years and an elected president every seven. This mattered for stability because Germany under the Kaiser had no written constitution at all and the Kaiser had made and changed laws as he pleased. The new system gave the Republic a claim on its citizens' loyalty that the old regime never had, and the first election in January 1919 drew an 82 per cent turnout, with the moderate SPD taking 40 per cent and the Centre Party 20 per cent. On this facet the constitution was a stabilising force [E].

**The second facet is proportional representation and the coalition governments it produced.** One seat was awarded for roughly every 60,000 votes, which guaranteed that smaller parties were represented in the Reichstag. The consequence was that no single party ever won a majority. There were nine coalition governments between 1919 and 1923 alone, and because policy had to be agreed between partners it lacked vision and took far longer to pass. A system that was designed to be fair therefore made decisive government almost impossible, and it did so precisely in the years when Germany faced reparations, the occupation of the Ruhr and hyperinflation. Here the constitution actively worked against stability [E].

**The third facet is Article 48.** This allowed the chancellor to ask the president to pass emergency laws without the support of the Reichstag. It was included as a safeguard for genuine crises, but it quickly became a substitute for government by consent: Ebert used it 63 times between 1923 and 1924, and the abuse of the article continued into the 1930s. The significance is that the constitution contained, in writing, a lawful route around parliament. Once ministers grew used to governing that way, the Reichstag's authority was steadily hollowed out from within [E].

**The fourth facet is what the constitution could not reach.** Its checks and balances were carefully designed to stop any one person taking ultimate power, and the Reichsrat could challenge laws unless two thirds of the Reichstag overruled it. None of this subdued the extremist parties, who went on attacking the Republic violently, and the government still had to rely on force to survive, as it did against the Spartacists in 1919. Constitutional design could regulate how power was exercised, but it could not by itself create acceptance of the Republic among those who rejected democracy altogether [E].

**Judgement.** Of these, Article 48 was the most important in the long run, because it was the mechanism through which parliamentary government was ultimately set aside [A]. But it only became important because of the second facet: proportional representation fragmented the Reichstag so thoroughly that emergency rule came to look like the only way to govern at all. The deeper impact of the constitution was therefore not any single clause but the combination of the two, which together made weak coalitions normal and rule by decree routine [A].

That judgement should be qualified. The Republic did survive the crises of 1919 to 1923 and then stabilised markedly after 1924 under the same constitution, which suggests the document was not fatal in itself. Its impact was to leave the Republic with very little margin for error, so that when a crisis as severe as the Depression arrived, the constitutional weaknesses that had been survivable in the 1920s became decisive [A].

parts.problem_md: Write an account of cultural developments in Weimar Germany during the 1920s.
parts.solution_md:
The Weimar years saw what is often called a cultural explosion. The government gave grants to artists and to cultural organisations such as theatres and libraries, and crucially it supported rather than censored new approaches to the arts. New technologies, particularly radio and film, gave German artists mediums that had not existed a generation earlier [R].

Painting moved in an experimental direction. Expressionist artists used grotesque and exaggerated figures in violent scenes, deliberately intending to make audiences uncomfortable so that they would question the society they lived in. Otto Dix, working in the New Objectivity style, produced work drawing attention to the difficulties faced by war veterans returning to Germany, including his 1927 piece Metropolis. George Grosz painted Grey Day in 1921, using expressionist techniques to convey the monotony of ordinary life [R].

Architecture and design were transformed by the Bauhaus movement, founded by Walter Gropius in Weimar in 1919. The school operated in three German cities, Weimar, Berlin and Dessau, between 1919 and 1933, and its teaching staff included the painter Paul Klee and the sculptor Oskar Schlemmer. Bauhaus design used geometric shapes to produce practical buildings, found beauty in technology, and used familiar materials in unfamiliar ways, going as far as constructing entire buildings from concrete. It inspired architects such as Erich Mendelsohn, who designed the Einstein Tower, an observatory at Potsdam built to resemble a rocket [R].

Cinema grew fastest of all. By 1929 there were roughly 500 cinemas across Germany, and German studios began to compete with American production. The Cabinet of Doctor Caligari, directed by Robert Wiene in 1920, was among the first horror films and contained what is generally regarded as the first plot twist ending in cinema. F. W. Murnau's Nosferatu of 1922 was the world's first vampire film. Metropolis, directed by Fritz Lang in 1926, was funded by the government through the organisation UFA at a cost of five million Reichsmarks, and used modernist science fiction to examine the effect of technology on modern life. Germany produced its first talking picture in 1930, and by 1932 some 3800 German cinemas could show films with sound [R].

City nightlife flourished alongside this. Berlin in particular offered cabaret, theatre and nightclubs, and these encouraged a far more liberal social atmosphere than pre-war Germany had known [R].

Not everyone welcomed the change. Extreme left-wing parties such as the KPD regarded government funding of culture as money that should have gone to workers in need. Extreme right-wing parties such as the NSDAP argued that Weimar culture was destroying German traditions and was responsible for a moral decline, and movements such as the Wandervogel campaigned for a return to traditional values. Weimar culture was therefore both one of the Republic's genuine achievements and one of the grievances its enemies used against it [R].

parts.problem_md:
The Weimar Republic tried to improve living standards in the 1920s.

How far did the lives of women improve in the Weimar Republic? Explain your answer.
parts.solution_md:
In law and in public life the change was dramatic [R]. The Weimar Constitution gave every woman over 21 the vote on exactly the same terms as men, which few European countries had done, and Article 109 declared marriage an equal legal partnership and gave women the right to enter all professions on an equal footing. German women used these rights rather than simply holding them: turnout among women voters was usually around 90 per cent, and 111 women were elected as party representatives to the Reichstag in 1920. A country that had been ruled by a Kaiser a few years earlier now had women helping to make its laws [E].

There was also a real change in how women could live [R]. More women worked as teachers and doctors, the retail sector took on large numbers of women part-time, and the 'New Woman' of the 1920s cut her hair short, wore make-up, smoked and drank in public and put a career ahead of becoming a wife and mother. These were freedoms no earlier generation of German women had enjoyed [E].

Against this, the position at work barely moved and in one respect went backwards [R]. In 1918 around 75 per cent of women were in employment; by 1925 that had fallen to about 36 per cent, roughly where it had been before the First World War. Many employers simply ignored Article 109 and appointed men, women who did hold jobs were paid about a third less than men doing equivalent work, and a woman was still expected to give up her job when she married. At the top the door stayed shut, and Germany had only 36 female judges as late as 1933. A legal right that employers can disregard is not the same as an improved life [E].

The gains also created their own opposition [R]. The right wing blamed the 'New Woman' for destroying the traditional family, Hitler argued she was taking jobs from working-class men and campaigned to send women back to the home, and the male-dominated trade unions resented 'double earners' because they believed equality for women would damage male workers. This matters because it meant the improvements were politically fragile rather than settled [A].

I partially agree that women's lives improved [A]. As citizens they gained more in a decade than in the previous century, and the vote, Article 109 and a real presence in the Reichstag are not small things. But most women experienced their lives through work and marriage rather than through the constitution, and there the improvement was thin: fewer women in jobs than in 1918, a third less pay, and a career that ended at the altar. The lives of women improved most in the areas the state could change by law, and least in the areas that depended on employers and on what society expected of them [A].

parts.problem_md:
The Weimar Republic tried to improve living standards in the 1920s.

Why did the Weimar Republic's welfare reforms benefit some Germans more than others?
parts.solution_md:
One reason is that the reforms were built around regular industrial employment [R]. The Unemployment Insurance Act of 1927 worked by diverting three per cent of the wages of 16.4 million workers into a fund, which then paid 60 Reichsmarks a week to anyone insured who lost their job or fell ill. A scheme funded out of wage packets can only protect people who receive wage packets. The other main gains worked the same way, since the working week was cut from 50 hours in 1925 to 46 in 1927 and real wages rose by 25 per cent between 1925 and 1928. All of this reached workers in towns and cities, and almost none of it reached a farm labourer or a smallholder [E].

A second reason is that farming was suffering from problems the reforms never touched [R]. Agricultural communities were caught between heavy debt, falling prices for what they produced and rising taxes, and no welfare measure addressed any of those three things. The result was that the gap widened rather than closed: while town workers were getting shorter hours, insurance and new housing, the income of agricultural workers fell to 44 per cent below the national average by 1929. Reforms that help one group while another group's underlying position gets worse will always look unfair to the second group [E].

parts.problem_md:
The Kaiser's Germany collapsed at the end of the First World War.

What happened in Germany during the revolution of November 1918?
parts.solution_md:
Unrest that had begun with a naval mutiny at Kiel spread across the country, and there were mass protests on the streets of Berlin [1]. In Munich the workers went on general strike on 7 November and declared Bavaria a separate communist state, while in Hanover soldiers joined the workers and rioted [1]. Councils of workers and soldiers were set up in many towns to replace the Kaiser's local authorities [1]. On 9 November the Kaiser's military advisers told him he had to abdicate, and the following day he escaped by train to the Netherlands [1].

parts.problem_md: Discuss the impact of political disorder in Weimar Germany between 1919 and 1923.
parts.solution_md:
Between 1919 and 1923, Weimar Germany had to face political disorder, which led to severe consequences and affected the survival and stability of the new republic. Trust and confidence of ordinary people in the government were influenced by extremist uprisings, political violence, and government responses [E]. In this essay, I will discuss how these factors impacted the Weimar government.

One important impact of political disorder was the shaking of public trust in the republic. The Spartacist uprising of 1919 was the first blow. The government hired the Freikorps to crush the uprising, due to which the republic looked weak to the people. The hiring of violent paramilitary groups further aggravated the situation [E]. There were some other left-wing revolts, such as the Ruhr Uprising of 1920, due to which many Germans were convinced that democracy was nothing but instability and chaos. Due to all these uprisings, the legitimacy of the new democratic system became questionable, and it seemed unable to defend itself without using violent methods [A]. The right-wing opposition also grew due to political disorder. The Kapp Putsch of 1920 and the Munich Putsch of 1923 also tried to overthrow the government, and revealed the nationalist groups that were growing in Germany [E]. Although both uprisings failed, they not only exposed the weaknesses of the government but also made it clear that parts of the army and judiciary were leaning towards the right. Another point to observe was that the right-wing rebels were punished lightly compared to the harsh treatment of the left-wing revolutionaries. This further established the belief that the Weimar Republic was fragile [A].

Secondly, the political disorder also led to economic consequences. It was immensely difficult to stabilise the economy or attract foreign investment when political turmoil was at its peak. After a missed reparations instalment, France occupied the Ruhr, and the Weimar government encouraged workers to go on strike. The government also printed extra currency to deal with economic problems, which led to hyperinflation [E]. During this phase many people lost their savings, and this created distrust of the government, especially among the middle class. Common people held the republic responsible for their hardships, which were exploited by extremist parties. Ideas such as the 'November Criminals' and the 'stab in the back' became popular at this time [A].

Lastly, daily activities such as schooling and community life were often disrupted by constant strikes, protests, and street fighting between different groups. In cities like Berlin, Munich and the Ruhr, families were worried about their safety as riots and violence became frequent [R]. There were shortages of food and basic goods, so people had to queue for hours to buy essentials such as bread. Malnutrition grew among poorer communities. Common people felt that life was chaotic and unpredictable, which contributed to frustration and tension [E].

On the other hand, it can be argued that even after political disorder, the Weimar government survived. Under Ebert's leadership, both left-wing and right-wing rebellions were suppressed. Due to this resilience the Weimar Republic survived until 1923, when Stresemann introduced reforms to stabilise Germany and establish some political and economic stability [A].

To conclude, the political disorder of 1919 to 1923 undermined faith in the Weimar Republic and strengthened extremist opposition. While the government did survive, the instability, violence and economic turmoil caused ordinary people to lose faith in democracy, which was later exploited by the Nazis [A].

parts.problem_md: Write an account of the Spartacist uprising in 1919.
parts.solution_md:
One of the biggest challenges the newly formed Weimar Republic faced was the Spartacist uprising that took place in January 1919 in Berlin. A radical left-wing group, the Spartacist League, led the uprising [R]. Its leaders, Karl Liebknecht and Rosa Luxemburg, were inspired by the Russian Revolution and Marxist ideology. The main aim of the uprising was to overthrow the German Republic, led by Friedrich Ebert, and set up a Soviet-style government in Germany. They envisioned a republic of workers' and soldiers' councils, or soviets, and equal sharing of wealth and power [E].

The immediate cause of the uprising was the dismissal of the left-wing police chief of Berlin, Emil Eichhorn, by Ebert on 4 January 1919. He was replaced by an MSPD minister. As a result, the Spartacists formed a Revolutionary Committee to plan the uprising and called for a general strike, staged protests and held demonstrations [R]. More than 100,000 workers took to the streets, seizing key buildings in Berlin such as newspaper offices and erecting barricades in the streets. The uprising was not a peaceful one, and there were violent clashes between government forces and the Spartacists [E].

Ebert had to seek help from the Freikorps, a right-wing group of former soldiers who strongly opposed communism, because the government did not have its own reliable army. He signed a deal with the Freikorps and used them and the army to crush the uprising [R]. The Freikorps used brutal force, not hesitating to fire on protestors with machine guns to crush the rebellion. Within a week the uprising was suppressed, resulting in the deaths of hundreds of workers [E]. On 15 January 1919 the Freikorps arrested and murdered the leaders of the Spartacist movement, Karl Liebknecht and Rosa Luxemburg. Their deaths were a serious setback to the communist movement in Germany. It also exposed how much the new Weimar Republic relied on right-wing military groups to maintain order [E].

The Spartacist uprising was a test for the Weimar Republic. Although it failed, it exposed the divisions in German society between communists, social democrats and right-wing forces. It also showed Ebert's dependence on the Freikorps, which would later pose its own threat to the stability of the Republic [E].
